title: New public charge rule takes effect Friday; Indian green card applicants face wider scrutiny
excerpt: Starting September 18, immigration officers gain broader discretion to weigh Medicaid, SNAP and school-meal use when deciding whether applicants could become dependent on government aid. Twenty-one states and D.C. sued this week to block the rule.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security's new "public charge" rule takes effect Friday, September 18, rescinding the 2022 Biden-era framework and restoring broader officer discretion to deny green cards and visas.
  • Immigration officers may now consider an applicant's — or a household member's — use of Medicaid, SNAP (food stamps) and school-meal programs, benefits the Biden rule excluded from review.
  • New York Attorney General Letitia James is leading 21 states plus D.C. in a lawsuit filed Monday in Manhattan federal court; NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani is leading a separate coalition of cities and counties.
  • For Indian applicants, the change matters most in family-sponsored cases: benefits used by a spouse, child or other household member can now factor into an officer's overall assessment.

A new federal rule that dramatically expands how immigration officers can hold an applicant's use of public benefits against them takes effect on Friday, September 18 — and 21 states plus the District of Columbia sued this week to stop it.

The Department of Homeland Security rule rewrites the "public charge" test, a provision of U.S. immigration law that lets officials deny a visa or green card to someone deemed likely to become primarily dependent on government assistance. The new policy rescinds the narrower 2022 Biden administration framework — which generally limited review to cash assistance and government-funded long-term institutional care — and restores the broader discretion immigration officers had under a 2019 Trump-era rule.

What the rule changes

Under the new rule, immigration officers can consider an applicant's use of Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and participation in school-meal programs as part of the applicant's overall circumstances. Officers may also look at benefits used by an applicant's child or another household member. The states' lawsuit argues the rule sets no clear limits on which benefits could count, leaving families guessing about what might jeopardize their status.

"Will getting health insurance hurt my chances of getting a green card? Will accepting food assistance when I fall on hard times be held against me?"

— New York Attorney General Letitia James, at a City Hall news conference on Monday

The states, whose lawsuit also includes the District of Columbia, argue they would lose billions of dollars in federal funding if immigrants — particularly in mixed-status families — disenroll from programs out of fear of immigration consequences, according to CNN's reporting.

The legal fight

James and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the two lawsuits at a City Hall news conference on Monday. The states' suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, argues DHS exceeded its authority and violated the Administrative Procedure Act. California Attorney General Rob Bonta is co-leading the challenge with James and Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, while Pennsylvania joined through Gov. Josh Shapiro.

DHS defended the policy in a July 16 post on X: "Under @POTUS Trump, DHS is restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves. We are reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers."

What it means for Indian applicants

Most employment-based Indian applicants — H-1B and L-1 professionals — rarely use the benefits in question, but the expanded discretion matters most in family-sponsored cases: spouses, parents and other relatives whose petitions an officer evaluates holistically. Because officers may now factor in benefits used by a child or household member, a family where one member used Medicaid or school meals could face tougher questions. The rule also reaches visa applicants abroad, which could affect consular decisions on family-visa cases processed in India.

Attorneys also warn of a chilling effect: families legally entitled to benefits may forgo them out of fear of immigration consequences. "This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, healthcare coverage and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled," James said in a statement. Her office noted it fought the 2019 version of this policy and won.

What's next

Barring a court injunction before Friday, the rule takes effect September 18. The states' lawsuits seek to block it in federal court — a fight that could stretch for months. Anyone with a pending green card or visa case, or plans to file one, should consult an immigration attorney about how benefit use by household members could affect their application.
